newsitem.title: USA: Dole nears end of campaign marathon.
newsitem.headline: Dole nears end of campaign marathon.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole headed Tuesday for the final, symbolism-rich events of his campaign-ending marathon blitz -- paying homage to Harry Truman and returning to his native Kansas to vote.
At a midnight stop at a bowling alley, Dole predicted an upset win before an enthusiastic crowd. "A lot of people are going to be surprised," he said.

Dole's stop in Iowa came on the fourth and last night of campaigning around the clock in a non-stop campaign push that began on Friday, was to end at noon on Tuesday, and was aimed at helping Dole snatch victory.
"It's been a great campaign," he said in Des Moines. "The bottom line is we are very optimistic."
From Des Moines, Dole was to travel to Independence, Missouri, to pay homage at a statute of the late Democratic President Harry Truman.
Truman's come-from-behind victory over Tom Dewey in the 1948 presidential election has become a political legend cited by struggling politicians of both parties as reasons to keep going.
"I may be the Harry Truman of 1996," he told radio talk show host Don Imus on Monday.

Dole has never led President Bill Clinton in the polls during the general election campaign, but some polls have showed a narrowing under Dole's assault on alleged violations of ethics by the Clinton administration.

In a Reuters/Zogby poll on Monday, Clinton's lead over Dole had widened again after narrowing over the weekend. Clinton moved up to a 7.3 percentage point lead 44.2 to 36.9 percent with Ross Perot at 7 percent and more than 10 percent undecided.
Other polls continue to show Clinton with a wide lead.
After the Independence stop, Dole was to rest for about four hours -- only the second such pause during the entire campaign push.

The last leg of the blitz would then take him back to the beginning of his political journey, his hometown of Russell, Kansas, cited repeatedly by Dole as the source of bedrock values that have fired his political career.
"This is the last crusade of a great warrior," Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain, a steady travelling companion of Dole's, said at the Des Moines rally.
Dole was to vote in Russell at about noon, then return to Washington to await the election results.

At a rally late Monday in a Knoxville, Tennessee, roadhouse, Dole told an overflow crowd that how well he fared in the election was no longer in his hands, but that voters angry with alleged White House ethical violations would carry him to victory.
"I really believe we're down to the time where probably nothing I would say would sort of change the election," Dole said.
Dole said voters have begun to focus on the election. "I think what they've concluded, very simple, is that character does matter. I've got a feeling the American people have had enough," he said.
The presidency should serve as a role model and source of inspiration, he said. "I want you to be proud of the vote you cast."
Fatigue showed in his weak gestures and a slow, measured voice, but determination also was evident as he doggedly pressed on.
But at other times, he showed energy and enthusiasm, bouncing, for example, to the pounding bass of the music in Des Moines.

And in an earlier appearance at the Vermilionville living history museum in Lafayette, Louisiana, Dole shrugged off the effects of non-stop campaigning and danced a Cajun two-step with his wife, Elizabeth.
Dole told reporters on his plane he would head straight for Florida, where he keeps a vacation condominum, after the election, regardless of whether he won or lost.
"Either way, you'll go to Florida?," Dole was asked.
"Oh, yeah," he said.
